test_title: PYST 09: RRB Group D Official Paper GS - (Held On: 01 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: A baby pulls a toy car along the ground. If the force and displacement are in the same direction, the work done is:

options.text: equal to the product of force and displacement
equal to the speed of the car

solution:
The correct answer is __**equal to the product of force and displacement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Work Done:** Work is defined as the product of the force applied to an object and the displacement of the object in the direction of the force. The formula for work is: **Work (W) = Force (F) × Displacement (d) × cos(θ)**, where θ is the angle between force and displacement.
 
• **Same Direction:** When the force and displacement are in the same direction, the angle θ between them is **0 degrees**. Hence, **cos(0) = 1**, and the work done simplifies to **W = F × d**.
 
• **Positive Work:** Since the force and displacement are aligned (same direction), the work done is positive. This means energy is being transferred to the object.
 
• **Real-Life Example:** In the given scenario, when a baby pulls a toy car along the ground with force and the car moves in the same direction, the work done is equal to the product of the force exerted and the displacement of the car.
 
• **Incorrect Options:** Option 1 (equal to zero) is incorrect because work done is zero only when there is no displacement or the force is perpendicular to the displacement. Option 2 (negative) is incorrect because work is negative when force and displacement are in opposite directions. Option 4 (equal to the speed of the car) is irrelevant, as speed is not related to work. Option 5 is not applicable in this case.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Factors Affecting Work Done:**

 
 
• **Force:** Work increases with the magnitude of the force applied.
 
• **Displacement:** The greater the displacement, the higher the work done.
 
• **Angle (θ):** The angle between force and displacement determines the effectiveness of the force. When θ = 90°, **cos(90) = 0**, and no work is done.
 
 
 
• **Units of Work:**
 
 
• The SI unit of work is the **joule (J)**, where 1 joule = 1 newton × 1 meter.
 
• Other units include the erg (in CGS system) and foot-pound (in FPS system).
 
 
 
• **Types of Work:**
 
 
• **Positive Work:** Occurs when force and displacement are in the same direction, transferring energy to the object.
 
• **Negative Work:** Occurs when force and displacement are in opposite directions, reducing the object's energy.
 
• **Zero Work:** Happens when there is no displacement, or the force is perpendicular to displacement.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Work:**
 
 
• In daily life, examples of work include lifting objects, pulling carts, and pushing furniture.
 
• In science, work is used to calculate energy transfer, such as in engines, machinery, and physical systems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Development:** The concept of work in physics was introduced by **Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis** in the early 19th century.
 
• **Conservation of Energy:** Work is closely related to energy transfer, and the principle of energy conservation states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.
 
• **Work and Power:** Power is the rate at which work is done, and its formula is **Power = Work/Time**. The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
 
• **Work and Kinetic Energy:** The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object is equal to its change in kinetic energy.
